title: Elderwood
summary: Elderwood, tracked as G0066 and also reported as the Elderwood Gang, Beijing Group and Sneaky Panda, was a long running espionage operation documented between roughly 2009 and 2016 against defence, aerospace, technology, human rights and non governmental organisations. Public reporting assessed the activity as linked to Chinese state interests, with the caveat that the name describes a campaign and overlapping tooling rather than a single proven team, so different vendors split the activity differently. Elderwood is historically important because investigators observed a shift from simple remote code execution exploits toward zero day vulnerabilities, in which the attacker uses a flaw before the vendor has a fix, and toward watering hole attacks. In a watering hole attack the group compromises a legitimate website that its targets are known to visit, then serves malicious content only to selected visitors. The campaign is also associated with supply chain abuse, where a trusted software update or installer carries the malicious payload. Evidence appears in web server logs of injected scripts, browser and plugin crash reports, endpoint records of unusual child processes started by documents, and network flows to compromised legitimate sites.

beginner.definition: Elderwood is the name for a long spying campaign that ran from about 2009 to 2016. It targeted defence companies, technology firms and human rights groups. Public reports linked the campaign to Chinese state interests, and other names for it include Beijing Group and Sneaky Panda.
beginner.whyItMatters: Elderwood changed how defenders think about trust. Instead of attacking you directly, the attackers poisoned a website you already visit or an update you already install. Nothing about the address looked wrong. This is why you cannot rely only on blocklists of bad sites. You also need to watch what happens after a page loads or an installer runs, because the danger may arrive through something that was genuinely trusted until the moment it was compromised.
howItWorks: The attackers pick targets such as defence firms, research groups or human rights organisations.
They find a website those targets visit often, then compromise that website.
They add hidden code (small instructions that run in your browser) to the site.
Only selected visitors receive the harmful content, so most people see a normal page.
The hidden code exploits a weakness in the browser or a plugin and installs a backdoor.
In some cases they instead tamper with a software update, so the payload arrives as a trusted install.
beginner.example: Picture a hospital coffee shop that staff and visitors trust. Someone breaks in at night and puts a few wrong pills inside the vitamin jar. Nobody suspects the shop, because the shop is familiar and everyone buys there daily. Only certain people get the wrong pills. Elderwood works like this. The website is the trusted shop, the hidden code is the wrong pill, and the attackers choose exactly who receives it.
takeaways: A trusted website can be compromised and used to reach you, so trust must be checked constantly.
A zero day is a weakness used before the software maker has released a fix.
Web server logs and browser crash reports often reveal watering hole activity.

objectives: Explain what the Elderwood campaign was and which sectors it targeted.
Define a watering hole attack and describe why selective delivery makes it hard to spot.
Explain what a zero day vulnerability is and how it changes a defender's options.
Describe how supply chain tampering with software updates delivers malicious code.
Identify the evidence sources used to investigate a compromised legitimate website.
